Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. DOCUMENT:
Policy Brief: Extending the Heat Pump Top-Up Grant Countywide
Climate and Environment Team, Harnley County Council, June 2026

1. Recommendation
That Cabinet extend the £2,500 local top-up grant for domestic heat pumps, piloted in two districts in 2025, to the whole county from April 2027, with a budget of £2.5 million a year for an initial two years.

2. Background
Domestic heating accounts for around a quarter of the county's carbon emissions, and most homes are heated by gas or oil boilers. The national boiler upgrade grant covers part of the cost of a heat pump, but survey evidence shows the remaining upfront cost is still the main barrier for households, with typical net costs of £4,000 to £7,000 after the national grant.

In January 2025 the Council launched a local top-up of £2,500 per installation in Ashby and Coleton districts, paid on top of the national grant. The top-up was available to owner-occupiers only, with the installation carried out by an accredited installer. The pilot ran for the full calendar year.

3. Results
Table 1. Heat pump installations, by district group
District group | 2024 installations | 2025 installations | Change
Pilot districts (Ashby, Coleton) | 140 | 238 | +70%
Other five districts | 210 | 252 | +20%
County total | 350 | 490 | +40%

Installations in the pilot districts grew by 70%, compared with 20% elsewhere. The top-up therefore caused around 50 percentage points of additional growth, and we expect a similar uplift in the remaining districts once the top-up is available countywide.

The pilot also had broader benefits. In March 2025 the regional installer training centre opened at Coleton College, and the number of accredited installers based in the two pilot districts rose from 9 to 23 over the year. Installers reported that the top-up gave them the confidence to recruit. Wait times for an installation survey in the pilot districts fell from around ten weeks to four.

Customer feedback was positive: of 196 households who completed the follow-up survey, 88% were satisfied or very satisfied with their heat pump, and 91% said the top-up was important in their decision.

4. Value for money
Grant payments in the pilot totalled £595,000 (238 installations at £2,500). Each heat pump replacing a gas or oil boiler saves about 2.1 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, so the 238 installations will save around 500 tonnes a year, or 7,500 tonnes over a 15-year equipment life. That is a cost to the Council of about £56 per tonne, well below the £120 per tonne threshold the Council uses to appraise climate investments.

5. Proposal
We propose a countywide top-up of £2,500 per installation, with the same eligibility and installer requirements as the pilot, capped at 1,000 grants a year (£2.5 million). On current trends, demand is likely to reach this cap in the first year. Because the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers, we expect demand from the private rented sector to remain a significant share of applications, which supports the Council's private-sector housing standards objectives.

Administration would continue to be handled by the existing two-person grants team, with one additional post funded separately from the Council's climate reserve. Grants would be paid directly to installers on completion, as in the pilot, to reduce the risk of fraud.

6. Risks
Installer capacity outside the pilot districts is lower, and waiting lists could lengthen if demand rises sharply. We will work with the training centre to promote accreditation in other districts.
If the national grant is reduced, the local top-up may be insufficient on its own to sustain demand. We will review the scheme annually.

7. Conclusion
The pilot shows that a modest local top-up substantially increases heat pump uptake, at a cost per tonne of carbon well within the Council's threshold. Extending it countywide is a cost-effective way to accelerate the decarbonisation of home heating.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "That is a cost to the Council of about £56 per tonne" -- £595,000 / 7,500 tonnes = about £79 per tonne, not £56. (Still under the £120 threshold, but the stated figure is wrong.)
2. [inconsistency] at: "Because the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers" -- Section 2 states the pilot top-up was available to owner-occupiers only; section 5 says the pilot was open to landlords as well. The eligibility rule contradicts itself.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "The top-up therefore caused around 50 percentage points of additional growth" -- The pilot districts differed in another major way: the document reports the regional installer training centre opened in Coleton in March 2025 and accredited installers there rose from 9 to 23, cutting survey wait times. Installer supply is a clear confounder, so the growth difference cannot be attributed to the top-up (and pilot districts were not randomly chosen).

REVIEW:
# Review: Heat Pump Top-Up Grant Brief

The brief's headline claims don't hold up. The causal claim is confounded, the cost-per-tonne figure contains an arithmetic error, and it treats every grant as an additional installation. With those corrected, the grant may still be worthwhile, but the brief doesn't show it clears the £120 threshold.

## 1. The 50-point uplift is not cleanly attributable to the grant

- **The training centre is a rival explanation.** Coleton College's installer training centre opened in March 2025, in a pilot district, during the pilot year. Accredited installers there rose from 9 to 23 and survey waits fell from ten weeks to four. More installers and shorter waits would raise installations with or without a grant. The brief presents this as a "broader benefit" of the top-up, but it is a separate supply-side change, and it is confounded with the treatment.
- **The installer testimony is circular.** "The top-up gave them the confidence to recruit" is self-report from parties who benefit from the grant, and it can't separate the grant from the training centre.
- **The comparison is weaker than "before-and-after with a benchmark" suggests.** It uses one pre-period, so there is no evidence of parallel trends. The pilot districts started from a different base (about 70 installs per district against about 42). The brief doesn't say how the districts were chosen. Spillovers into the comparison districts are also possible.
- **"Far too large to be chance" is untested.** No test is reported, and with 98 and 42 extra installs the numbers are small. Chance is also not the main risk. Bias is.
- **The survey cannot show causation.** The 91% who said the top-up was "important" are grant recipients, and people who received money tend to say it mattered. This is stated attribution with no counterfactual. The 88% satisfaction figure is irrelevant to whether the grant works.

## 2. The value-for-money figure is wrong, twice

**Arithmetic error.** The brief's own inputs give £595,000 ÷ 7,500 tonnes = **£79 per tonne**, not £56. That is about two-thirds of the threshold, not "less than half".

**Additionality is ignored.** The calculation credits all 238 installs to the grant. Using the brief's own comparison:

- Without the grant, the pilot districts would have grown about 20%, to roughly 168.
- Additional installs are about 70, not 238.
- Additional savings are 70 × 2.1 t × 15 years ≈ 2,200 tonnes.
- Cost per additional tonne is £595,000 ÷ 2,200 ≈ **£270**, more than double the £120 threshold.

For the grant to meet £120 per tonne, about two-thirds of the 238 installs (roughly 157) would need to be additional. The brief's own estimate is about 70, and that is an upper bound once the training centre is accounted for.

Other gaps:
- The carbon saving of 2.1 t a year is described as "standard". It should state its source and whether it allows for grid decarbonisation, which reduces savings over a 15-year life.
- There is no discounting.
- Administration costs are excluded.
- There is no sensitivity analysis.

## 3. Internal inconsistencies

- **Eligibility.** Section 2 says the pilot was for owner-occupiers only. Section 5 says it "was open to landlords as well" and builds the private-rented-sector argument on that. Both can't be true, and the brief says eligibility stays "the same as the pilot". The inconsistency also affects the budget and the landlord split-incentive question.
- **The demand forecast.** The cap is 1,000 grants a year, but the whole county installed 490 in 2025. Applying the pilot uplift to the other five districts gives roughly 357 there, plus about 240 in the pilot districts, so about 600 in total. "Likely to reach this cap in the first year" is unsupported. Either the cap is too high, or demand would need to double, which conflicts with the installer capacity concerns.

## 4. "Proven, same design" overstates it

- The training centre and its local installer pool won't exist in the other five districts, which the brief itself says have lower capacity.
- Scaling from 238 to up to 1,000 grants with the same two-person team plus one post is a large administrative jump, with no workload analysis.
- Nothing addresses whether a countywide grant would be partly absorbed into higher installer prices.
- Two years of £2.5m is a firm commitment, so this is a real scale-up, not a continuation of an experiment.

## 5. Risks are thinly mitigated

The author says each risk has a mitigation. For national policy the only one is an annual review, which doesn't mitigate anything. For installer capacity it is "promote accreditation", with no targets, funding or timeline. There is no exit or trigger point, such as pausing if waits exceed a set number of weeks.

## What would make the case defensible

1. Correct the arithmetic and present cost per tonne under several additionality scenarios (100%, the DiD estimate, and a lower figure that adjusts for the training centre).
2. Separate the grant effect from the training centre, for example by comparing Ashby against Coleton, or by looking at monthly installs before and after March 2025.
3. Resolve the owner-occupier and landlord contradiction.
4. Base the demand and budget forecast on the pilot data, and justify the 1,000 cap.
5. Consider a phased rollout, which would also generate better evidence than a simultaneous countywide launch.
6. Add concrete risk triggers and mitigations.

The pilot may well show the grant helps. The brief currently claims much more than the data can support, and a Cabinet member checking the sums would find the £56 figure doesn't reproduce.
